learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected The truck pushes harder and locked the prediction for a 10,000 kg truck and 1,000 kg car. Before locking, the accessibility container already said each vehicle feels 389 kilonewtons; the visual pre-prediction state was not separately inspected.
observations.exploration: Moved to 100 ms: both forces were 18 kN, while truck and car speed changes were 2.4 and 24.0 m/s. Played to 120 ms: zero force and final changes 2.4 and 24.1. Set truck mass to 1,000 kg at the final state: both speed changes became 13.2 m/s.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to equal forces, explained opposite interaction forces and mass-dependent acceleration, and accurately used the current equal-mass final changes of 13.2 m/s each.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot at 100 ms with the heavy truck. Equal opposing force arrows were both labelled 18 kN; unequal thin velocity arrows and separate speed-change readouts distinguished the effects.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The concrete misconception is useful, but the accessible pre-prediction description leaks equality.
prediction.evidence: Before locking, the container said each vehicle feels the same 389 kilonewtons.

interaction.reason: Time and mass controls distinguish force equality from unequal effects and an equal-mass boundary.
interaction.evidence: The tenfold mass ratio gave tenfold speed-change contrast; equal masses gave equal changes.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains both laws and adapts accurately to the current boundary case.
payoff.evidence: It quotes 13.2 m/s for both equal masses and states a = F / m.

clarity.reason: Different arrow roles and explicit values separate force from velocity.
clarity.evidence: At 100 ms both forces read 18 kN while speed changes differed sharply.

transfer.reason: The general interaction rule is stated without a fresh noncollision application.
transfer.evidence: Only the same vehicle collision is varied.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: The smaller car pushes just as hard while undergoing a much larger speed change.
surprise.evidence: The heavy-truck case shows equal force and about tenfold speed-change difference.

visualExplanation.reason: The paired arrows expose equal causes and unequal responses.
visualExplanation.evidence: Equal force labels sit over visibly unequal velocity arrows.

playfulness.reason: Time scrubbing and mass variation provide a useful physical toy.
playfulness.evidence: The equal-mass adjustment changes the outcome without changing the force rule.

practicalValue.reason: It clarifies a common confusion between force and effect.
practicalValue.evidence: The reveal distinguishes interaction equality from acceleration.

depth.reason: The lesson links Newton's third law with mass-dependent acceleration.
depth.evidence: The equal-mass boundary complements the original unequal-mass case.

complexity.reason: The visual is familiar, but force, velocity and speed change must be kept distinct.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Moderate: equal interaction forces do not imply equal acceleration.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: time slider, play button and mass slider.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: Separate a force pair from its different effects on different masses.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Newton's third law and acceleration formula are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Moderate: kN, kg, ms, m/s and different arrow meanings.

whyCool: The dramatic asymmetry of the collision survives even when the pushes are exactly equal.
caveat: The accessible pre-prediction description reveals equality. The ideal collision and speed changes do not model injury or structural damage.
missingEvidence: The visual pre-prediction state was not separately inspected.
